lesson.title: Turning Voltage into Area: The Op-Amp Integrator
lesson.summary: Replacing the feedback resistor of an inverting amplifier with a capacitor produces a circuit whose output tracks the running integral of its input, the electronic equivalent of accumulating area under a curve over time.
lesson.body:
Recall the inverting amplifier: a virtual ground sits at the inverting input, held there by negative feedback, and the gain is set by the ratio of the feedback resistor to the input resistor. Now ask what happens if the feedback element is not a resistor but a capacitor.

Because the inverting input sits at a virtual ground and draws no current into the op-amp itself, whatever current flows in through the input resistor R has nowhere to go except onto the feedback capacitor C. That current charges the capacitor, and since a capacitor's voltage is its accumulated charge divided by capacitance, and charge is the time integral of current, the output voltage ends up proportional to the running integral of the input voltage, with a negative sign because the current flows into the inverting side. This is the same charging relationship covered under the capacitor and RC circuit concepts, now happening deliberately at a virtual ground instead of a floating node, with the op-amp forcing that virtual ground to hold steady no matter how much charge piles up on the capacitor.

The result is Vout(t) = -(1/RC) times the integral of Vin dt, plus whatever voltage the capacitor started with. The product RC is the same time constant introduced in the RC circuit concept, now setting how aggressively the circuit integrates rather than how fast it charges toward a fixed level.

Take R = 10 kilohm and C = 1 microfarad, so RC = 10,000 times 0.000001 = 0.01 second, or 10 milliseconds. Suppose the capacitor starts fully discharged, Vout(0) = 0V, and a constant Vin = 1V is applied starting at t = 0, a DC step. Since the input is constant, its integral is just that constant times elapsed time, so Vout(t) = -(1/0.01) times 1V times t = -100t, in volts, with t in seconds. At t = 1 millisecond (0.001s): Vout = -100 times 0.001 = -0.1V. At t = 10 milliseconds (0.01s): Vout = -100 times 0.01 = -1.0V. The output is a straight downward ramp at a constant rate of -100V per second, exactly what "integrating a constant produces a ramp" means in concrete volts and seconds.

Real integrators need periodic help. Any tiny DC offset at the op-amp's input integrates without bound over time, since even a very small constant error still produces a ramp, and that ramp eventually drives the output into saturation against the supply rails. Practical integrator circuits add a large resistor or a reset switch across the capacitor to bleed off this accumulated drift periodically. The differentiator circuit, covered next, has almost the opposite problem.
